idiom_name: hand-written binding-power table over an enum token stream
implementation_notes: Swift ships no parsing facility, so the Pratt table is hand-written: an enum Token, an indirect enum (or class) for the expression tree, a rule lookup carrying binding powers, and a recursive parseExpr(minBp:) that throws a positioned diagnostic - the same structure as the C and C++ forms, expressed with pattern matching and value types. The ecosystem shows a model worth copying: custom operators are declared against precedence groups (infix operator +-: AdditionPrecedence), and swift-syntax's own parser first builds a flat SequenceExprSyntax of operands and operators and applies precedence afterwards, so when the target syntax is Swift-like or must be re-parsed incrementally, reuse SwiftParser/SwiftSyntax instead of re-deriving the folding. Choose the hand-written table for small DSLs inside an app where pulling in swift-syntax would outweigh the loop.
pitfalls: A recursive expression tree needs an indirect enum or a class; without it the type does not compile, and switching representation later changes the public API.

precedencegroup declarations and custom infix operators configure Swift's own compiler for your types - they do not supply a parser for a different grammar, so relying on them for a DSL is a category error.
Value semantics make parser state copyable: a parselet that captures self by value can keep operating on a stale parser, so parser state must be a reference type or always passed inout.
